title: CSS Grid
in30Seconds: CSS Grid is CSS's two-dimensional layout system. A grid container defines columns and rows; its direct children become grid items that can be placed into the resulting cells or made to span several tracks. Set `display: grid` on the parent, then describe its tracks with properties such as `grid-template-columns` and `grid-template-rows`. Grid is useful when both horizontal and vertical structure matter.
whyItMatters: Grid gives a page or component an explicit spatial plan instead of relying on offsets and coincidences. In coursework, its terms—container, item, track, line, and area—make layout decisions testable and explainable. In practice, a named grid can keep a header, navigation, main content, and supplementary content coherent as the design evolves. This lesson focuses on Grid's rows, columns, lines, areas, and sizing; flexbox and responsive adaptations are separate subjects.
learningObjectives: Define grid container, grid item, track, line, and area.
Explain how explicit columns and rows create a grid.
Distinguish line placement from named-area placement.
Apply `fr`, `repeat()`, and `minmax()` to a simple track definition.
Calculate a simple `fr` allocation after fixed tracks are removed.

collegeVersion.heading: A two-dimensional formatting context
collegeVersion.body:
An element with `display: grid` establishes a grid formatting context. Its direct children are grid items; deeper descendants are not automatically items of that same grid. Grid is two-dimensional because the container has a column axis and a row axis. A column or row is a grid track, and the dividing boundaries are grid lines. The rectangle between adjacent row and column lines is a grid cell. One or more cells together form a grid area. These names are diagnostic tools: when an item appears in the wrong place, ask which lines, tracks, or area the rule actually addresses. The container controls this arrangement; setting a placement property on an item does not convert that item into a new parent grid for its own descendants.

The author can define an explicit grid with `grid-template-columns` and `grid-template-rows`. For example, `grid-template-columns: 12rem 1fr;` makes two explicit column tracks: a fixed 12rem first track and a second track that receives the remaining available space as a flexible fraction. If items need more slots than the explicit grid supplies, Grid can create implicit tracks; `grid-auto-rows` and `grid-auto-columns` control their size. This lesson uses explicit tracks so that placement is visible and intentional.

collegeVersion.heading: Placing items with lines and areas
collegeVersion.body:
Grid offers more than one readable placement language. Line placement uses `grid-column` and `grid-row`. In a three-column grid, `grid-column: 1 / 3` places an item from column line 1 up to, but not including, line 3, so it spans two column tracks. Line numbers refer to boundaries, not the tracks themselves. The end line can also be expressed with `span`, as in `grid-column: 1 / span 2`. An item without an explicit placement participates in the auto-placement algorithm. Author-defined names can also be attached to grid lines when a design benefits from a more meaningful placement vocabulary.

Named areas make a larger page pattern easier to inspect. `grid-template-areas` writes a row-by-row diagram using names, and an item joins a named rectangle through `grid-area`. Every repeated name must make a rectangle; an L-shaped repetition is invalid for a named area. Areas are particularly useful when the layout has meaningful regions such as `header`, `nav`, `main`, and `aside`. They do not replace semantic HTML: a landmark element still needs appropriate HTML structure. Grid describes placement, while HTML communicates document meaning.

collegeVersion.heading: Sizing tracks deliberately
collegeVersion.body:
Track lists can mix fixed lengths and flexible sizes. The `fr` unit represents a share of leftover space in the grid container after fixed-size tracks and gaps are accounted for. Thus `1fr 2fr` divides the available flexible space into three equal shares, assigning one to the first track and two to the second. It does not mean a fraction of the entire viewport, and content constraints can affect an actual used size. `repeat(3, 1fr)` is a compact way to write three equal flexible tracks.

`minmax(min, max)` gives a track a range. For example, `minmax(12rem, 1fr)` says a track should not be smaller than 12rem and may take a flexible share up to its maximum behavior. Grid's sizing algorithm considers intrinsic content contributions and constraints, so a classroom calculation should state its simplifying assumptions. `gap` creates deliberate separation between tracks; it is not a column or row itself. A fixed length, a percentage, an intrinsic size keyword, and a flexible fraction answer different sizing questions; do not replace one mechanically with another. In particular, an item's unbreakable content may impose a minimum that makes a simplified fraction calculation unsuitable for a production layout. When debugging, inspect the computed grid, identify fixed and flexible tracks, and then distinguish a sizing question from a placement question. Do not use this lesson as a substitute for flexbox, media-query, or container-query decisions.

vocabulary.definition: An element that establishes a grid formatting context with a grid display value.
A direct child that participates in its parent grid container's layout.
A column or row between two adjacent grid lines.
A dividing boundary that can be used to place or span grid items.
The smallest grid unit, bounded by adjacent row and column grid lines.
A rectangular region made from one or more grid cells.
A flexible fraction that shares leftover grid space with other flexible tracks.
Tracks created by Grid when placement needs extend beyond the explicit grid.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Imagine a bulletin board ruled into rows and columns. The board owner decides how wide each column and how tall each row should be. A note can occupy one square, or stretch across several squares. CSS Grid gives a web page that kind of board. The parent makes the board; its direct children are the notes placed on it. You can point to the board's boundary lines, or give a rectangular region a name such as `main`.

Some columns can have a fixed width, while others share the room left over. A `1fr` track gets one share; a `2fr` track gets two shares when the board has flexible space to divide. That is why Grid is helpful when a layout needs both rows and columns planned together.
eli10.analogy: Grid is like a labeled bulletin board with ruled rows and columns, where notes can occupy named rectangles or span boundary lines.
eli10.analogyLimits: A real grid layout also follows CSS sizing rules, content minimums, and auto-placement. The board analogy does not calculate those rules or provide HTML meaning.

workedExample: A dashboard container uses `display: grid; grid-template-columns: 160px 1fr 2fr; gap: 20px;`. Assume its content box is 800px wide and ignore content minimums. The fixed first column uses 160px. Two gaps use 40px, leaving 600px of flexible space. The remaining tracks have 1 + 2 = 3 fraction shares, so the second track receives 200px and the third receives 400px. A summary card with `grid-column: 2 / 4` starts at line 2 and ends before line 4, spanning the second and third tracks. It does not occupy the gaps as tracks; the gaps remain separation between tracks.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling every descendant a grid item.
commonMistakes.correction: Only direct children of the grid container are items in that grid.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a line number as a track number.
commonMistakes.correction: Lines are boundaries; placement from line 1 to line 3 spans two tracks.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming `fr` is a fixed percentage of the viewport.
commonMistakes.correction: Flexible fractions share leftover space after applicable fixed sizing and gaps.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using named grid areas as HTML semantics.
commonMistakes.correction: Use semantic HTML for meaning; areas only describe layout placement.

compareContrast.distinction: A line is a boundary; a track is the row or column space between adjacent lines.
Explicit tracks come from the template; implicit tracks are created when placement requires more tracks.
Line placement addresses numbered or named boundaries; named-area placement addresses a declared rectangular region.

keyTakeaway: CSS Grid plans rows and columns together. Define tracks, then place direct-child grid items by lines or named areas while treating flexible sizing as a share of leftover space.

questionBank.prompt: After a parent receives `display: grid`, which elements are that grid's items?
questionBank.explanation: A grid container lays out its direct children as grid items. Deeper descendants belong to their immediate parent unless it establishes another grid.

questionBank.prompt: What does `grid-column: 1 / 3` do in an explicit grid?
options: Uses only the first column track
Starts at line 1 and spans to line 3, covering two column tracks
questionBank.explanation: Grid-column uses boundary lines. The interval from line 1 to line 3 contains two tracks.

questionBank.prompt: A 800px grid has columns `160px 1fr 2fr` and two 20px column gaps. Ignoring content constraints, how wide is the `2fr` track?
questionBank.explanation: After 160px and 40px of gaps, 600px remains. Three fraction shares split it into 200px shares, so 2fr is 400px.

options: It can define an L-shaped area with one repeated name
It works only with fixed pixel tracks
A repeated area name must form a rectangle
questionBank.explanation: Named grid areas must be rectangular. They describe layout rather than adding HTML semantics.

questionBank.prompt: What is an implicit grid track?
options: A track created when placement needs extend beyond the explicit grid
A named area in the HTML document
questionBank.explanation: The implicit grid supplies tracks beyond the template when item placement requires them; it is neither a gap nor an area.
